Apex Industrial Machinery Corp. - Q2 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Industrial Machinery Corp. Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star two. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Apex Industrial Machinery Corp.'s results for the Q2 2024. Joining me on today's call are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Rivera, Chief Financial Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on Apex Industrial Machinery Corp.'s performance for the Q2 2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts, and I'd like to highlight a few key achievements. First, we've achieved a record backlog of $4.2 billion, up 22 percent year-over-year, reflecting robust demand across our core segments like automation and precision machining. Second, our book-to-bill ratio strengthened to 1.28 times, signaling strong order momentum and multi-quarter visibility into shipments. Third, operating margins expanded meaningfully by segment, with our industrial automation business hitting over 21 percent, driven by high-margin robotics and digital solutions. Fourth, we've optimized inventory levels to $1.75 billion, with turns improving to 4.2 times, freeing up substantial working capital through lean strategies. And fifth, we're raising our full-year revenue guidance, underpinned by tailwinds in electrification, semiconductors, and reshoring.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Rivera to provide more detail on our financial results.

Michael Rivera (CFO):
Thank you, Johnathan. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining our Q2 2024 earnings call for Apex Industrial Machinery Corp., or AIMC. As your CFO, I'll walk you through our top-line performance, which underscores the resilience and momentum in our manufacturing and industrial equipment portfolio amid a dynamic macroeconomic backdrop. I'll start with total revenue and year-over-year growth, then cover book-to-bill trends, operating margin performance by segment, inventory levels and management strategies, before closing with our outlook for Q3 and full-year 2024.

Starting with the headline numbers: For the second quarter, we delivered total revenue of $2.58 billion, representing a robust 14.2 percent year-over-year increase, or 12.8 percent on an organic constant-currency basis excluding the impact of our recent acquisition of TechForge Robotics. This marks our eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth and positions us at the high end of the industrial equipment peer set, outpacing Caterpillar's recent full-year growth and aligning closely with Rockwell Automation's performance in their automation-heavy segments.

Diving deeper into the drivers, our growth was propelled by a healthy mix of volume expansion, pricing discipline, and mix shift toward higher-margin aftermarket and digital solutions. Equipment sales, which comprise about 58 percent of our revenue mix, came in at $1.50 billion for the quarter—up 17 percent year-over-year—fueled by strong demand for our next-gen CNC machining centers and precision automation systems. Average selling prices rose 4.2 percent year-over-year, reflecting steel and component pass-throughs amid lingering supply chain inflation, but also premium pricing on our IoT-enabled SmartForge series, which now accounts for 35 percent of machine bookings. Our order backlog stands at a record $4.2 billion, up 22 percent year-over-year, with lead times extending to 14 months for high-spec electro-hydraulic presses—signaling robust capex cycles in end-markets like automotive OEMs reshoring EV battery gigafactories.

Aftermarket parts, service, and digital revenue—our highest-margin bucket at 32 percent of the mix—grew 12 percent year-over-year to $825 million in Q2, driven by elevated utilization rates averaging 82 percent across our installed base of over 150,000 machines globally. This reflects customers prioritizing uptime amid labor shortages, with uptake in our AI-powered predictive maintenance platform surging 45 percent year-over-year. Subscription revenue from this platform hit $120 million annualized run-rate, up from $75 million last year, mirroring trends we've seen at peers like Siemens in their MindSphere ecosystem.

Regionally, performance was broad-based but highlighted pockets of strength. North America contributed 42 percent of Q2 revenue at $1.08 billion, up 18 percent year-over-year, benefiting from the CHIPS Act-fueled semiconductor fab builds and IIJA infrastructure spend—think new orders from Intel and TSMC's Arizona plants for our wafer fab polishing equipment. EMEA, at 28 percent of the mix or $722 million, grew 11 percent year-over-year despite headwinds from the Ukraine-related energy crunch; we offset this with share gains in wind turbine nacelle assembly lines, capturing 15 percent market share in offshore renewables. APAC was the star, delivering $680 million or 26 percent of revenue—up 16 percent year-over-year organically—with China rebounding to 8 percent growth post-COVID lockdowns on semiconductor and solar polysilicon demand, while India and Southeast Asia exploded 25 percent on Make in India incentives for CNC lathes serving Foxconn's iPhone lines. LatAm rounded out at 4 percent of the mix with modest 5 percent growth, tempered by mining cyclicality in Brazil.

Strategically, these results validate our Industrial Renaissance initiative—$450 million invested year-to-date across Industry 4.0 tech stacks, including edge computing for real-time OEE optimization and hybrid-electric drivetrains reducing fleet emissions by 30 percent. This not only boosted our book-to-bill ratio to 1.25 times but also de-risked us from tariff volatility, with 75 percent North American content in our U.S.-built machines. Compared to the broader Gardner Intelligence index, where industrial machinery output grew just 9 percent globally, our outperformance stems from proactive supply chain diversification—dual-sourcing rare earths from Australia and Vietnam—and a 20 percent year-over-year increase in R&D spend targeting AGV fleets for warehouse automation, a $15 billion TAM growing at 22 percent CAGR per McKinsey.

Now, let's turn to our book-to-bill ratio and the underlying trends, as this metric remains a critical leading indicator of our demand pipeline and future revenue visibility in our cyclical industry. For those new to our story at AIMC, the leading provider of precision CNC machining centers, robotic automation systems, and smart factory solutions for the industrial equipment sector, the book-to-bill ratio is calculated as total orders booked divided by total revenue recognized—or billed—in the quarter. A ratio above 1.0 signals that we're booking more orders than we're shipping, building backlog and providing multi-quarter visibility. In the manufacturing and industrial equipment space, where lead times for complex systems like our high-precision 5-axis CNC mills or collaborative robot arms can stretch 6 to 12 months, this metric is particularly telling amid supply chain volatility and end-market shifts.

In Q2, we delivered a robust book-to-bill of 1.28, up sequentially from 1.15 in Q1 and marking our strongest reading since Q4 2022. On a trailing 12-month basis, it's now 1.22, reflecting sustained demand momentum. Bookings totaled $3.30 billion in the quarter, a 14 percent increase quarter-over-quarter and 22 percent year-over-year, outpacing our $2.58 billion in revenue recognition. This drove backlog growth to that record $4.2 billion, up 18 percent from year-ago levels, giving us exceptional visibility into fiscal 2025—over 90 percent of our guidance already locked in.

Breaking down the key trends and drivers: In automation and electrification tailwinds, our book-to-bill in the factory automation segment hit 1.45, fueled by surging orders for our next-gen AI-optimized robotic welders and palletizing systems. Demand from EV battery gigafactories—partners like Tesla's Texas expansion and Northvolt's U.S. plants—accounted for 25 percent of bookings, up from 15 percent a year ago. Similarly, semiconductor equipment makers like Applied Materials and Lam Research are ramping capex for advanced nodes, boosting orders for our precision metrology tools. Aerospace recovery showed a ratio of 1.32, with Boeing and Airbus suppliers front-loading orders for our titanium-machining centers amid 737 MAX and A320neo production ramps. Traditional markets like heavy machinery and general industrial held steady at 1.10, as customers like Caterpillar and Deere digest inventory from last year's over-ordering.

Regionally, North America, at 55 percent of bookings, posted a book-to-bill of 1.35—our standout region—driven by CHIPS Act-funded semi-fabs such as Intel's Ohio site and reshoring initiatives. The IRA's clean energy incentives are accelerating orders from battery and solar OEMs, with lead times extending to 9 months due to skilled labor constraints. Europe, 25 percent, had a 1.20 ratio, resilient despite energy headwinds; German auto giants like Volkswagen and BMW are investing in Industry 4.0 upgrades for electric drivetrains. Asia-Pacific, 15 percent, dipped to 1.05 from 1.18 last quarter as Chinese fabricators work through excess inventory in consumer electronics, though Taiwan semi remains a bright spot at 1.40 with TSMC's Arizona spillover benefiting us, and India's Make in India push added significant new orders for textile and pharma automation. Rest of world was flat at 1.10, with LatAm mining equipment holding firm.

Technical initiatives fueling the backlog include our IndustroAI platform—our proprietary edge-computing software integrated into 80 percent of new systems—which has shortened programming times by 40 percent for end-users, driving upsell; 35 percent of bookings included AI/ML upgrades, commanding 15 to 20 percent premiums. Capacity expansions like our new 250,000 square foot facility in Spartanburg, South Carolina, are on track for Q4 startup, adding 20 percent to CNC output. We've secured long-lead components like linear guides from THK and servos from Yaskawa, mitigating tariff risks. Sustainability push saw orders for our energy-efficient GreenLine series—certified for EU Carbon Border Adjustment—surge 30 percent, appealing to ESG-focused customers like Siemens.

Strategically, this greater-than-1.2 times book-to-bill underscores our positioning in secular growth pockets: automation with projected 8 to 10 percent CAGR per McKinsey, electrification, and digital twins. We're prudently managing turns—expecting 3.8 times inventory turns in fiscal 2025—while quoting conservatively to protect margins at 28 to 30 percent. Risks include potential U.S. election policy shifts on subsidies or prolonged China inventory cycles, but our 65 percent U.S. and Europe revenue mix derisks us versus pure Asia plays.

Next, I'd like to spend a few minutes on inventory levels and our management strategies, which have been a key focus amid the ongoing volatility in the industrial equipment sector. Our disciplined approach here not only supported our record revenue but also drove a 150 basis point expansion in gross margins to 32.5 percent, while freeing up $250 million in working capital compared to last year.

At quarter-end, our consolidated inventory stood at $1.75 billion, flat sequentially from Q1 but down 8 percent year-over-year. This reflects our targeted inventory turnover ratio of 4.2 times for the quarter—above our long-term goal of 4.0 times and a meaningful improvement from 3.6 times in Q2 2023. In terms of days of inventory on hand, we're at 87 days, down from 102 days a year ago and within our optimal 85 to 90 day band. For context, this outperforms the industry average of 105 days, as reported in the latest Deloitte manufacturing benchmark, and positions us favorably against peers like Caterpillar.

Breaking it down by segment, our core machinery division—CNC lathes, hydraulic presses, and automated assembly lines—saw inventories decline 12 percent year-over-year to $950 million, driven by robust order fulfillment rates above 98 percent. Raw materials and work-in-progress made up 55 percent of total inventory, finished goods 35 percent, and MRO spares the balance. Notably, our high-value electrification products, like the next-gen EV battery assembly robots, represent just 15 percent of inventory value but 40 percent of bookings, underscoring our shift toward higher-margin, lower-volume SKUs.

On trends, inventory built modestly in early 2024 due to supply chain headwinds—steel lead times stretched to 20 weeks from 8, and semiconductor shortages for our PLC controls delayed shipments by 15 percent. But we've reversed that trajectory. Sequential days on hand improved by 5 days in Q2, fueled by a 20 percent ramp in production efficiency from our new Monterrey facility. End-market diversification—into renewables and data center cooling systems—has stabilized backlogs at 14 months.

Regionally, North America, accounting for 55 percent of our inventory base, tightened to 82 days—our best in three years—thanks to localized sourcing from U.S. steel mills amid Section 301 tariffs. EMEA, 25 percent, held steady at 92 days; we're navigating energy transition tailwinds, with wind turbine gearbox inventories optimized via just-in-time kanban with suppliers like Siemens Gamesa. APAC, our growth engine at 20 percent, ticked up to 105 days due to front-loading components ahead of anticipated U.S.-China trade escalations and disruptions in Southeast Asia, though our Shanghai fab's output surge cut electronics WIP by 18 percent.

Turning to strategies—these are core to our Lean 2.0 initiative, which has delivered $400 million in cumulative savings since 2022. First, advanced demand sensing and forecasting: We've rolled out AI-driven tools on our SAP S/4HANA platform, integrating IoT data from 5,000-plus machine sensors and external signals like PMI indices and steel futures. This has slashed forecast error from 25 percent to 12 percent for our top 80 percent SKUs, enabling dynamic safety stock adjustments; our EOQ models now factor real-time volatility, reducing order quantities by 15 percent without service level hits.

Second, supplier ecosystem optimization: Over 60 percent of our $1.2 billion direct materials spend is under vendor-managed inventory programs with partners like Nucor for steel plate and TSMC for control chips. We've consolidated our supplier base from 1,200 to 850, with dual-sourcing for critical inputs—steel now has 95 percent on-time delivery versus 75 percent last year. In Q2, this unlocked $120 million in early-pay discounts at a blended 1.5 percent rate.

Third, digital thread and traceability: RFID and blockchain pilots across our Greenville, South Carolina, and Pune plants track 90 percent of WIP in real-time, cutting obsolescence by 30 percent—critical for long-lead items like precision gears with 24-month shelf lives. We're also leveraging generative AI for scenario planning, such as modeling a 20 percent steel price spike from Red Sea disruptions, which informed our Q3 build plan, holding raw steel stocks at 45 days versus a 60-day norm.

Strategically, we're balancing service levels—targeting 99 percent on-time delivery, up from 96 percent—with working capital discipline. Inventory as a percentage of revenue is now 18 percent, down from 22 percent in 2023 and below Ingersoll Rand's level. This discipline funded $300 million in share repurchases year-to-date without touching our revolver. Looking forward, we see opportunities to trim another 5 to 7 percent in the second half via accelerated factory digitization, including our $50 million investment in Epicor Kinetic ERP extensions for multi-plant visibility. Risks include persistent inflation in aluminum and labor tightness in Mexico, but our hedging—80 percent of next year's metals exposure—is in place. On the upside, CHIPS Act subsidies for domestic semi-fab will derisk electronics inventory by 2025.

Now, turning to operating margin performance by segment, which underscores the resilience and improving profitability profile of AIMC as we navigate a volatile macro environment. Overall, our consolidated adjusted operating margin expanded 210 basis points year-over-year to 14.2 percent, marking the strongest Q2 performance in five years. This reflects a favorable product mix shift toward higher-margin aftermarket services and automation solutions, disciplined cost management through our Enterprise Lean Sigma program, and pricing actions averaging 4.2 percent across the portfolio—more than offsetting 2.8 percent input cost inflation from steel, aluminum, and copper.

Sequentially, margins held steady from Q1's 14.0 percent, despite seasonal destocking in our Heavy Machinery segment. FX headwinds, particularly a stronger USD against the EUR and CNY, shaved about 30 basis points off the top line, but our hedging program mitigated 70 percent of that impact. Let me break this down by our four reporting segments: Industrial Automation, Heavy Machinery, Precision Components, and Energy Systems.

Starting with Industrial Automation, which represented 28 percent of Q2 revenues at $1.2 billion—up 12 percent organically—adjusted operating margins surged 340 basis points to 21.4 percent, our highest in the cycle, driven by 15 percent volume growth in factory floor robotics and PLC systems powering reshoring at customers like Tesla and Intel fabs. Pricing contributed 150 basis points, with our new Gen-4 collaborative robots commanding a 10 percent premium due to embedded AI for predictive maintenance. Cost leverage was key: COGS as a percentage of sales improved 4 points to 62 percent, thanks to our digital twin initiative simulating production lines to optimize throughput—yielding a 22 percent reduction in scrap rates at our Rockford, Illinois facility. North America led with 25 percent growth and 23 percent margins from IRA-driven semiconductor capex; EMEA dipped to 19 percent on energy surcharges but rebounded via localized sourcing; APAC held at 20.5 percent despite softer China demand. We're gaining share from ABB and Fanuc in cobot deployments, targeting 25 percent segment margins by fiscal 2025 through software-as-a-service upselling, where recurring revenue now hits 35 percent of segment mix.

Shifting to Heavy Machinery, 35 percent of revenues at $1.5 billion—flat organically amid mining destocking—margins expanded 180 basis points to 12.8 percent, reflecting 5 percent pricing gains on excavators and wheel loaders as infrastructure spend ramps under the U.S. IIJA and EU's NextGenEU programs. Mix shift helped: aftermarket parts and services grew 18 percent to 42 percent of segment revenue, with higher 25 percent-plus margins versus OEM equipment at 8 to 10 percent. Our ValueStream Optimization program—leveraging IoT sensors for fleet telematics—cut maintenance downtime 30 percent for customers like Rio Tinto, enabling upsell of service contracts. Steel costs rose 6 percent year-over-year, but forward contracts and a 15 percent shift to high-strength, lower-alloy steels from Nucor contained it to a 50 basis point headwind. North America shone at 14.5 percent margins on data center construction; LatAm faced 10 percent pressure from copper volatility in Peruvian mining; APAC was flat at 11.5 percent from Australian coal slowdowns. We're positioning for a second-half inflection with backlog up 20 percent on autonomous haul truck pilots, aiming to mirror Caterpillar's margin trajectory.

Precision Components, 22 percent of revenues at $950 million—up 8 percent organically on aerospace recovery—margins improved 120 basis points to 16.7 percent, propelled by favorable aircraft OEM mix—Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320neo ramp-ups—and 7 percent pricing on CNC-machined titanium parts for GE Aviation engines. SG&A leverage from shared services shaved 80 basis points, with automation of our multi-axis mills boosting yield 12 percent via machine learning defect detection. Supply chain wins included dual-sourcing forgings from U.S. and Indian mills, dodging Red Sea disruptions. Raw material inflation was muted at 1.5 percent thanks to LME hedging. North America drove 19 percent margins on defense primes like Lockheed Martin; EMEA at 15.5 percent with Airbus localization; APAC challenged at 14 percent from EV battery softness. Our pivot to additive manufacturing with laser powder bed fusion targets 20 percent margins by reducing part counts 40 percent in hydraulic actuators—early wins position us against Howmet Aerospace.

Finally, Energy Systems, 15 percent of revenues at $650 million—up 10 percent on LNG demand—margins rose 250 basis points to 13.5 percent, driven by 12 percent growth in gas turbine upgrade kits for Siemens and Baker Hughes, plus wind turbine gearboxes amid offshore expansion. Pricing added 100 basis points, with hybrid hydrokinetic turbines fetching 15 percent premiums for U.S. DOE grants. Our BladeRunner predictive analytics platform cut gearbox failures 28 percent, enabling 30 percent service margin uplift. Copper wire costs eased 3 percent quarter-over-quarter, offset by epoxy resin inflation—contained via recycling pilots. North America led at 15 percent on Permian frac pumps; Middle East/EMEA at 14 percent with QatarEnergy LNG; APAC at 11 percent pressured by China's coal pivot. We're capitalizing on energy transition: electrification kits for drilling rigs, with renewables now 25 percent of backlog.

In aggregate, these dynamics delivered $420 million in segment operating income, up 22 percent year-over-year. After corporate costs and a one-time restructuring credit, we hit that 14.2 percent consolidated margin. Key tailwinds: 300 basis points from volume, mix, and pricing; 150 from productivity, offset by 100 in inflation and FX. We're on track for full-year margins of 13.8 to 14.3 percent.

Gross margin was 32.5 percent, driven by favorable product mix, pricing actions, and volume leverage. Operating expenses were $1.2 billion, resulting in an operating income of $500 million. Our net income for the quarter was $380 million, or $2.15 per share.

As we wrap up a solid quarter, I'm pleased to provide our outlook for Q3 and the full fiscal year 2024. Our guidance reflects robust underlying demand in core end-markets like automotive OEMs, aerospace, and semiconductors, tempered by some near-term headwinds in inventory digestion and supply chain normalization.

For Q3 2024 revenue guidance: $2.75 billion to $2.95 billion. We expect Q3 revenue to grow 12 percent to 20 percent sequentially from Q2, and 9 percent to 15 percent year-over-year. This range assumes a book-to-bill ratio holding steady at 1.15 times, driven by our strength in high-margin automation and precision machining segments. Key drivers include order intake momentum: backlog at $4.2 billion, with 60 percent visibility into Q3 shipments. We've seen particular strength in our ApexFlex CNC lathes and multi-axis mills, gaining share in EV battery manufacturing lines—integrations with Tesla's Gigafactory expansions and Ford's BlueOval City. Orders from semiconductor fab equipment makers added significant volume.

Segment breakdown: Automation and Robotics, $1.12 billion to $1.24 billion, up 18 percent year-over-year, with IoT-enabled systems like our ApexLink platform seeing 25 percent adoption growth and partnerships with Rockwell Automation accelerating deployment. Precision Machining, $880 million to $960 million, up 12 percent, with reshoring tailwinds in North America and demand for 5-axis VMCs up 15 percent amid CHIPS Act funding. Heavy Industrial Equipment, $600 million to $640 million, up 5 percent, softer in legacy steel but offset by hydraulic press sales to aerospace like Boeing 737 ramp-ups. Aftermarket and Services, $100 million to $120 million, up 8 percent, with recurring revenue from predictive maintenance subscriptions growing 30 percent year-over-year.

Regionally: North America, 55 percent of Q3 mix, expected to deliver 15 percent year-over-year growth, fueled by onshoring; U.S. industrial production PMI above 50 supports this, with wins at GM's EV plants and data center cooling equipment makers. EMEA, 25 percent, flat to plus 3 percent; energy transition in wind turbine components provides upside, but German auto slowdowns like VW's ID.4 cuts and Ukraine disruptions cap growth. Asia-Pacific, 20 percent, plus 10 percent, led by China's semiconductor rebound and India's PLI scheme boosting orders for our fiber laser cutters.

Gross margins should expand 150 basis points sequentially to 32.5 to 33.5 percent, aided by favorable FX with USD strength versus EUR and JPY, and volume leverage on our new Monterrey facility ramping to 20 percent of Mexico output.

Full-year 2024 revenue guidance: $10.6 billion to $11.0 billion. We're raising this from the prior range, now implying 10 percent to 14 percent growth over 2023's $9.67 billion. This embeds Q4 at $2.8 billion to $3.0 billion, reflecting seasonality and backlog conversion. At the midpoint of $10.8 billion, we're positioned for our strongest top-line year since 2019.

Strategic tailwinds: Our $150 million capex plan includes scaling ApexAI, our edge-computing suite for real-time spindle monitoring—reducing unplanned downtime by 25 percent for customers like John Deere's tractor lines; early wins have secured $300 million in multi-year contracts. Electrification and sustainability: 35 percent of Q3 orders tied to green capex, including electric arc furnace upgrades mirroring Nucor's expansions and lightweighting for eVTOLs. Supply chain resilience: inventory turns improved to 4.2 times; strategic sourcing from Vietnam offsets China tariff risks, with lead times down 20 percent on critical components like linear guides and servos.

Risks to monitor include potential softening in non-auto discretes if ISM new orders dip below 45, prolonged Boeing issues impacting aero aftermarket, and input cost inflation on rare earths. That said, our diversified exposure—only 25 percent auto OEMs—and 45 percent gross margin trajectory by year-end give us strong downside protection.

We're executing on our Machinery 2030 strategy: double digital services revenue to $200 million by 2026, expand Mexico and India footprints to 25 percent of capacity, and target 15 percent-plus EPS CAGR.

We are reaffirming our guidance for the full year, with expected revenue growth of 12 percent and EPS of $8.50 to $9.00. We are committed to returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Now, I will hand over to Lisa Chen, COO, for an operational update.

Lisa Chen (COO):
Thank you, Michael. Operationally, we've been focused on streamlining our supply chain and improving manufacturing efficiency. We've implemented several new initiatives from our Lean 2.0 program that are already yielding positive results, including AI-driven demand forecasting integrated with IoT sensors across our plants, which has reduced forecast errors and optimized safety stocks. We're closely monitoring the global supply chain situation—dual-sourcing critical components like servos and linear guides from partners in Vietnam and Australia—and taking proactive steps to mitigate disruptions, such as vendor-managed inventory for 60 percent of direct materials and RFID traceability to cut WIP obsolescence. Capacity expansions in Monterrey, Mexico, and Spartanburg, South Carolina, are ramping ahead of schedule, adding output for high-demand CNC and robotics lines. We are also investing in automation and digital technologies, like our ApexAI platform and digital twins, to enhance operational capabilities, boost OEE, and support 99 percent on-time delivery targets. These efforts have improved inventory turns to 4.2 times and shortened lead times by 20 percent on key items, positioning us well for backlog conversion amid reshoring and electrification trends.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. Our first question comes from David Wong with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

David Wong (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you discuss the impact of rising raw material costs on your profitability?

Michael Rivera:
Thanks, David. Rising raw material costs, particularly steel up 6 percent year-over-year, aluminum up 10 percent quarter-over-quarter, and copper volatility, have been a headwind we've actively managed. Input cost inflation totaled 2.8 percent across the portfolio, but our pricing discipline—averaging 4.2 to 5 percent gains—more than offset this, contributing 300 basis points to margin expansion. We've locked in forward contracts covering 80 percent of next year's metals exposure, shifted to high-strength lower-alloy steels with suppliers like Nucor, and utilized LME hedging for aluminum and copper. In heavy machinery and energy systems, this contained the impact to just 50 to 100 basis points. Vendor-managed inventory and early-pay discounts unlocked $120 million in savings, while productivity from digital twins reduced scrap by 22 percent in automation. Overall, these strategies supported 210 basis points of operating margin growth to 14.2 percent, with gross margins expanding to 32.5 percent. We're well hedged for Q3 and see no material risk to our full-year outlook.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter (JPMorgan):
What is your outlook for demand in the aftermarket services business?

Johnathan Hale:
Good question, Emily. Demand in aftermarket services remains a bright spot, representing 32 percent of our Q2 revenue mix at $825 million, up 12 percent year-over-year, and our highest-margin area. Utilization rates across our 150,000-machine installed base averaged 82 percent, driving uptake in AI-powered predictive maintenance—subscriptions hit a $120 million run-rate, surging 45 percent. Customers are prioritizing uptime amid labor shortages, with 30 percent growth in recurring revenue from platforms like ApexLink and BladeRunner, which cut downtime by 25 to 30 percent for users like Rio Tinto and John Deere. Aftermarket book-to-bill is over 1.3 times, with 42 percent of heavy machinery revenue now from parts and services. Tailwinds include Industry 4.0 upselling, where 35 percent of new bookings include SaaS elements commanding 15 to 20 percent premiums, and ESG-driven demand for GreenLine upgrades. We expect continued double-digit growth in H2, targeting double digital services revenue by 2026 under Machinery 2030, providing margin downside protection even if OEM softens.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Robert Kline with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Robert Kline (Morgan Stanley):
Can you provide an update on your progress in reducing lead times?

Lisa Chen:
Absolutely, Robert. Lead times have improved 20 percent overall on critical components like linear guides, servos, and precision gears, now averaging 14 months for high-spec presses and 9 months in North America, down from 18-month peaks post-COVID. This stems from our supply chain diversification—dual-sourcing from Vietnam, Australia, and Mexico offsets China risks—and securing long-lead items early with partners like THK and Yaskawa. The Monterrey facility ramp has boosted production efficiency by 20 percent, while IndustroAI and generative AI scenario planning optimize build schedules. Inventory turns at 4.2 times and JIT kanban with Siemens Gamesa for EMEA have tightened days on hand to 87 globally, with North America at a three-year low of 82 days. Just-in-time fulfillment rates exceed 98 percent, supporting 99 percent on-time delivery. Capacity adds in Spartanburg will further compress times for CNC output by Q4. Risks like Red Sea disruptions are modeled in our SAP system, but reshoring and CHIPS Act flows give us strong visibility—90 percent of FY25 guidance locked.

Operator:
Thank you. There are no further questions at this time.

Johnathan Hale:
Thank you for your questions and your interest in Apex Industrial Machinery Corp. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Jenkins:
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
